terms.definition: A nerve cell specialized to send and receive electrical and chemical signals.
terms.function: Receives, integrates, and transmits signals that make up the nervous system's communication network.
terms.whereItIs: Found in the brain, spinal cord, and nerves throughout the body.
terms.whyItMatters: Every thought, feeling, movement, and memory depends on neurons firing signals to one another.

terms.definition: The main part of a neuron containing the nucleus, where the cell's core life-support functions happen.
terms.function: Integrates incoming signals from the dendrites and houses the organelles that keep the neuron alive.
terms.whereItIs: The wide central bulb the dendritic tree and axon both attach to.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the neuron's control center — without it managing the cell's DNA and energy needs, the rest of the neuron couldn't function.

terms.definition: The structure inside a cell that holds its DNA and directs which proteins the cell builds.
terms.function: Stores the neuron's genetic instructions and directs protein production needed to build and maintain the cell.
terms.whereItIs: Inside the cell body (soma), visible when the soma is cross-sectioned or shown semi-transparent.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the instruction center for everything the neuron builds and repairs over its lifetime.

terms.definition: A small bean-shaped organelle that produces the ATP energy a cell needs to do its work.
terms.function: Produces the ATP energy the neuron needs to fire signals and to maintain the ion gradients that make firing possible.
terms.whereItIs: Near the base of the soma, close to where the axon begins.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a steady energy supply, a neuron couldn't reset its ion balance and would quickly stop being able to fire.

terms.definition: A branch-like extension of a neuron that receives signals from other neurons.
terms.function: Catches incoming chemical signals from neighboring neurons and carries them toward the cell body.
terms.whereItIs: The branching, tapering tree extending out from one side of the soma.
terms.whyItMatters: Dendrites are the 'listening end' of the neuron — more branching means a neuron can gather input from more neighboring cells.

terms.definition: The long, thin fiber of a neuron that carries a signal away from the cell body toward other cells.
terms.function: Carries the neuron's electrical signal (action potential) from the cell body all the way to the axon terminals.
terms.whereItIs: The single long shaft extending from the soma, opposite the dendrites.
terms.whyItMatters: The axon is the 'sending end' of the neuron — its length lets a single cell body signal targets far away, from the spinal cord to a toe.

terms.definition: A fatty layer wrapped around many axons that insulates them and speeds up signal travel.
terms.function: Insulates segments of the axon so the electrical signal jumps quickly between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier) instead of leaking away.
terms.whereItIs: Wrapped in sausage-link segments around the axon shaft, past the unmyelinated axon hillock.
terms.whyItMatters: Myelin is why some signals travel over 100 meters per second — damage to it, as in multiple sclerosis, slows reactions and can cause numbness.

terms.definition: The branching end of an axon where it connects to the next cell and releases neurotransmitters.
terms.function: Converts the arriving electrical signal into a chemical signal by releasing neurotransmitters toward the next cell.
terms.whereItIs: The branching cluster of small bulbous endings at the far end of the axon.
terms.whyItMatters: This is where an electrical signal becomes a chemical one — the handoff point that lets one neuron's message reach the next.

terms.definition: The tiny gap between two neurons (or a neuron and another cell) where a signal is passed on, usually using chemical messengers.
terms.function: Provides the junction where neurotransmitters released by an axon terminal cross the gap and bind to the next cell's dendrites, continuing the signal.
terms.whereItIs: The small gap between an axon terminal and a neighboring cell's dendrite or membrane.
terms.whyItMatters: Neurons don't touch — the synapse is where the entire nervous system's cell-to-cell communication actually happens, and it's the target of many medicines.

terms.definition: A chemical messenger released at a synapse that carries a signal from one neuron to the next.
terms.function: Crosses the synaptic gap and binds to receptors on the next cell, passing the signal along chemically.
terms.whereItIs: Released from the axon terminal into the synapse.
terms.whyItMatters: Neurotransmitters are how caffeine, many medicines, and neurological conditions change the way neurons communicate.
